newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-German oil sale plan draws fire, hits prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German oil sale plan draws fire, hits prices.

text.p: Germany on Thursday confirmed plans to sell crude oil from emergency reserves to help plug holes in government finances, drawing stern criticism from the West's energy watchdog and adding to pressure on world prices.

Bonn said it hoped to raise 400 million marks ($230 million) this year and an undisclosed amount in 1998 by selling oil stockpiled since the late 1970s as a way of cutting its budget deficit to qualify for European economic and monetary union.

The Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA), established by the major industrial nations in the wake of the 1974 oil price shock to protect its 24 members against future crises, condemned the decision.
"The IEA deeply regrets reports from Bonn today that the German government has decided to sell... oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserves (SPRs)," said IEA executive director Robert Priddle.
"The reported decision by Bonn -- coupled with the series of recent and forthcoming American sales -- sets a regrettable example to other IEA members."
Under emergency reserve obligations signed in 1975, IEA members are required to hold at least 90 days of net imports and release oil in the event of serious market turmoil.

If the German government sells its entire strategic crude oil reserve of 7.3 million tonnes, an option first mooted by economics minister Guenter Rexrodt last month, reserves held on behalf of German oil companies would still meet the agency's minimum requirement.

Germany is Europe's most oil-import dependent economy, relying on foreign supplies for 97 percent of consumption. Last year, it imported 2.1 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude and about 650,000 bpd of refined products like gasoline and heating oil.

While any relaxation of energy security policy was bound to trouble the IEA, analysts said the strength of its response was aimed at other members who may be looking at ways of raising revenue but whose stockpiles may be less ample.
"The IEA is seeking to discourage other member countries from following the same path," said Peter Bogin of Cambridge Energy Research Associates (CERA) in Paris.

The IEA said several other members have allowed their stocks to dip slightly below the 90-day level, a trend which if left unchecked could undermine the energy security programme last implemented during the Gulf War in 1991.

Priddle said a plan by a U.S. House of Representatives committee to sell $209 million worth of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in 1998, following three sales in the last 18 months, was equally disturbing.
"Following that reduction, the IEA calculates that U.S. SPRs will stand below 70 days of net imports," he said.

Industry sources said Bonn's proposed sale would release at least 75,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil at current prices -- equivalent to the output of a medium-sized North Sea field -- on to a market already beginning to buckle under the weight of rising supply.

World oil prices sank below $18 a barrel, shedding 27 cents to $17.95 a barrel by 1700 GMT, as the news of the sale added to downward pressure generated by evidence that Baghdad may be edging towards a resumption of limited oil exports under a U.N. oil-for-food accord.
"The timing is immaculate but if the German government believes (oil) prices are going lower then it makes sense for them," said Geoff Pyne, oil analyst at Swiss bank UBS.
